children.text: The debate over full-practice authority (FPA) for nurse practitioners and, increasingly, physician assistants, has moved from professional turf to empirical policy evaluation. With 27 states and D.C. now granting NPs FPA, a decade of implementation evidence allows researchers to distinguish the conditions under which scope expansion actually closes access gaps from those in which it produces minimal change.

The research on full practice authority (FPA) for nurse practitioners generally finds that loosening scope-of-practice restrictions modestly improves access to primary care in underserved areas, with the largest gains where FPA is paired with Medicaid reimbursement parity; where parity is absent, measured access gains are smaller and less consistent.
Full-practice authority without Medicaid reimbursement parity is a permission slip without a paycheck. The access gains only materialize when NPs can build financially viable independent practices.
Feasibility Conditions That Drive or Suppress Impact

body.title: FPA Impact Conditions: Factors That Amplify or Suppress Rural Access Gains

children.text: Multiple states have active FPA legislation, and some rural hospital associations that historically opposed these bills have shifted to support them — a change driven largely by how expensive and difficult physician recruitment in rural markets has become.

The remaining political opposition is concentrated in state medical associations and some specialty societies. The most effective legislative strategy observed in successful FPA states has been data-sharing agreements between NP associations and rural hospital coalitions that document specific unfilled positions that NP FPA would address—converting an abstract policy debate into a concrete vacancy count.

FEASIBILITY VERDICT: FPA legislation is a high-probability access intervention only when packaged with Medicaid reimbursement parity and NP-owned practice authorization. Standalone FPA without these co-conditions has insufficient evidence to justify the political capital required for passage.

children.text: Recommendations for State Health Policy Teams
Bundle FPA legislation with explicit Medicaid reimbursement parity provisions
Conduct rural vacancy audit before legislative introduction to build stakeholder coalition
Include hospital privileging reform in the legislative package to prevent post-FPA access suppression
Model 3-year access impact projections using Health Affairs FPA evidence base for fiscal notes

summary: Twenty-seven states now grant full independent practice authority to nurse practitioners, yet rural patient access improvements have been uneven. This feasibility study examines the fiscal, workforce, and political conditions under which scope-of-practice expansion produces measurable access gains in rural primary care deserts versus conditions where the policy produces minimal effect.
title: Expanding Scope of Practice for Rural NPs and PAs: A Feasibility Analysis of Full-Practice Authority Legislation
